system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2128-12-01 19:50:00 to 2128-12-02 17:07:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: An elderly female with a history of chronic diastolic heart failure, hypertension, dementia, and chronic pain presented with worsening head, neck, chest, and abdominal pain over one week. She and her son were concerned about a possible urinary tract infection recurrence due to prior associations between infections and pain flares, though no infection was found. She was treated with acetaminophen, IV fluids, and potassium supplementation. Her elevated lactate improved with hydration, hyponatremia resolved, and supratherapeutic INR was managed by holding warfarin with follow-up instructions. Imaging showed no acute intracranial, pulmonary, or abdominal pathology. Her pain improved significantly, and she was discharged home in stable condition with plans to resume warfarin after anticoagulation clinic follow-up.
problems: Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Other diuretics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain and diarrhea for a few days. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about three days ago. It’s sharp and all over, and I’ve had several loose stools. I also feel like I need to go to the bathroom more, but it hurts when I do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned pain with urination—any fever, chills, or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. A little nausea, but no vomiting now. I just feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs and urine. Your potassium is quite low at 2.6, which can cause weakness. We’re giving you fluids and potassium through the IV to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, low potassium can definitely make you feel that way. We’re correcting it, so you should start feeling better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan showed mild diverticulosis, but no sign of diverticulitis or other serious issues. Your chest X-ray shows some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—likely from not breathing deeply due to the abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious. It should improve as your pain gets better. We also found a urinary tract infection. That could be contributing to your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Will antibiotics help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We started IV antibiotics, but since you’re doing better, we’ll switch you to oral ciprofloxacin. You’ve had Klebsiella UTIs before, and this antibiotic works well for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your potassium is now 3.7—much better. You haven’t had any loose stools since yesterday, and your pain has improved. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. But what about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine culture grew a lot of bacteria, but it was contaminated with stool, so we can’t be sure of the exact type. Still, we’re confident cipro will treat it. Take it for three more days at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you today. We’re lowering your warfarin dose to 1 mg because of the antibiotic—it can increase the blood-thinning effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop my water pill? I usually take furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during your stay because of the low potassium. Your primary doctor will decide when to restart it. Just follow up with them in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your metoprolol and pantoprazole. We’re sending you home with acetaminophen for pain and instructions to monitor your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You improved quickly with fluids and antibiotics. Just finish the cipro and get your INR checked soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll take cipro twice a day for three days, warfarin at 1 mg daily, and resume your other meds except furosemide for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No furosemide until I see my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you develop fever, worsening pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. You did really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly female with a history of chronic diastolic heart failure, hypertension, GERD, and recurrent DVT/PE on warfarin presented with three days of diffuse abdominal pain, diarrhea, and dysuria. She was found to have hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and a urinary tract infection. Imaging showed diverticulosis without diverticulitis and bibasilar atelectasis likely due to splinting from abdominal pain. She was treated with IV fluids, potassium repletion, and antibiotics, initially for presumed viral gastroenteritis and confirmed UTI. Her symptoms improved rapidly, potassium normalized, and she tolerated a regular diet. Warfarin was reduced to 1 mg daily due to antibiotic interaction, and furosemide was held. She was discharged home in stable condition with a three-day course of oral ciprofloxacin, instructions to follow up on INR and medication management, and advised to monitor for weight gain or worsening symptoms.
